summary:
Cameroon criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 347-1 of the penal code, which carries a sentence of up to five years' imprisonment. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, and Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise them; reporting places Cameroon among the states in Africa with the highest prosecution rates. There is no legal gender recognition procedure and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation.

Appearance alone has served as the basis for prosecution. In November 2011 a Cameroonian court jailed Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome for five years after they were seen wearing women's clothes and ordering Baileys, with the original judge citing their dress, speech and the drink as proof that they were gay. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013. Defence lawyer Alice Nkom said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcomed the acquittal. Arrests made on grounds of effeminacy or appearance under the colonial-era sodomy law have carried sentences of six months to five years.

The February 2021 prosecution of the trans woman Shakiro (born 29 July 1997 in Douala, a YouTuber and activist with a substantial online following) is the clearest documentation of how the law reaches visibly gender-nonconforming people. She and her friend Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing and were convicted of attempted homosexuality, indecent dressing and identity-document irregularities. A Douala court sentenced each to five years, the maximum statutory term, plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs (about $370), on 12 May 2021 reporting, with an appeal filed. Lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu called the judgment a political decision made with no proof of any acts. Shakiro described five months of what she called hell in Douala's central prison, held initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; she subsequently left Cameroon to claim asylum abroad, and has since been granted asylum in Belgium. Her case and exile form part of Cameroon's record of criminalisation prosecutions.

Human Rights Watch reported on 11 May 2022 that violence against LGBTI people had risen sharply: from 9 March 2022 onward, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, over alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, and gendarmes beat two of them in detention. HRW senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi framed the pattern as a consequence of the statute itself, which lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence. Police violence and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and beatings of gay and trans people in public are reported as common. US State Department reporting as far back as 2010 recorded discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prison conditions and arbitrary arrests, describing the criminalisation context of Article 347.

For a visitor: visible trans expression in a public place is treated in practice as a prosecutable offence, arrests have been made on the strength of clothing, speech and drink orders rather than any observed act, and detention carries a real risk of beatings. No legal mechanism exists in Cameroon to recognise a trans person's gender, and no protection machinery covers anti-trans violence.
tangentialFactors:
The prohibition is colonial in origin: reporting on the 2013 acquittals describes the underlying sodomy law as colonial-era, and the 2016 penal code carried the ban forward in explicit statutory language rather than replacing it. Cameroon's position is comparable to that of the 30 other African states that criminalise same-sex relations, though its prosecution rate is at the high end of that group.

Outcomes are not uniform. The 2013 appeals-court acquittal of Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, welcomed by Amnesty International, shows that convictions resting on appearance and stereotype can be reversed, while the Shakiro judgment shows the same evidence base producing the maximum statutory term. The involvement of lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu, and of Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, indicates an active but narrow defence and monitoring presence.

Shakiro's public profile matters to her case: she is a Cameroonian trans activist who built a Facebook and YouTube following discussing trans life before her 2021 arrest, and her subsequent exile is part of the same documented pattern. Adjacent background from US State Department reporting lists killings, torture, harsh prisons and arbitrary abuses by security forces alongside anti-gay discrimination, situating LGBTI mistreatment within a broader record of abuse rather than a distinct regime.

Nothing in the sources indicates that general street crime, transport, entry formalities or other travel logistics differ for trans visitors from what applies to any traveller; those are outside this assessment.
localsOnly:
Cameroonian residents live under the same Article 347-1 exposure as visitors, but with no exit route: gender-nonconforming residents have been arrested in their own neighbourhoods and restaurants, and the Shakiro judgment demonstrates that a residence in Douala offers no protection against a five-year term for how a person dresses.

Residents face abuse from both sides of the enforcement line. HRW documented that in the period from 9 March 2022 security forces arrested and detained LGBTI people who were themselves victims of group attacks, rather than investigating the attackers, and that gendarmes beat two detainees. The researcher's assessment is that the statute licenses civilians and security forces alike to act with impunity.

No procedure exists for a Cameroonian to change legal gender markers on national documents, and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime law protects residents on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Detention itself is a documented hazard: held in Douala's central prison for five months, Shakiro was kept initially in leg chains and described the period as hell, conditions consistent with the harsh-prison and arbitrary-arrest findings in US State Department reporting from 2010. Residents convicted under the statute carry a criminal record that constrains them indefinitely, and those who fled, as Shakiro did, do so by claiming asylum abroad.
outOfScopeNotes:
Several points remain unresolved or unsourced. The outcome of the appeal against the Shakiro and Patricia sentence is not stated in the sources; only that an appeal was filed and Shakiro was released pending it. Her asylum grant in Belgium is not independently corroborated within this inventory beyond the record carried forward here.

Whether the at least six people arrested and eleven detained by security forces in the period Human Rights Watch described from 9 March 2022 were charged, convicted or released is not sourced. Nor is the number of prosecutions brought annually under Article 347-1: the claim that Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates is carried without a figure.

The exact current wording and full penalty range of Article 347-1 are not reproduced in the sources; only the five-year maximum is documented. The six-month-to-five-year range for arrests on effeminacy or appearance grounds comes from 2013 reporting and may reflect the colonial-era statute rather than the 2016 penal code. It is unresolved whether the 2013 acquittal established any binding precedent.

Nothing in this inventory addresses passport or visa screening of gender markers at Cameroonian entry points, availability of healthcare for trans visitors, or which specific facilities are accessible; these are not sourced and should not be inferred from the legal findings above.
